title: Virtualization Concept Map
subtitle: From one physical server to many virtual ones: hypervisors, containers, and VMware ESXi. Tap a bubble.
rootDesc: Virtualization runs several isolated computers on one physical machine by putting a software layer between the hardware and the operating systems. Almost every server in a modern data center is virtual, which is why an analyst investigating 'a server' is usually looking at a virtual machine on a hypervisor such as VMware ESXi.

modules.title: Why Virtualize?
modules.desc: Physical servers used to run one application each and sat mostly idle. Virtualization shares one machine's CPU, memory, disk, and network among many isolated systems.

children.title: Consolidation
children.desc: Dozens of virtual servers on a handful of physical hosts. Less hardware, power, cooling, and rack space.

children.title: Isolation
children.desc: Each virtual machine has its own operating system. A crash or compromise in one does not directly affect the others.

children.title: Speed
children.desc: A new server is created in minutes from a template instead of ordering and racking hardware — the reason test servers can be spun up for a single project.

children.title: Snapshots & recovery
children.desc: Save a machine's state before a change and roll back if it fails. Whole VMs can be backed up and restored as files.

children.title: Mobility & availability
children.desc: Running VMs can move between hosts without downtime, and restart automatically on another host if one fails. VMs can also be replicated to a disaster recovery site.

children.title: Labs
children.desc: Safe, disposable environments for testing patches, training, or analysing malware without risking real systems.

modules.title: Virtual Machine
modules.desc: A complete computer made of software: virtual CPU, memory, disk, and network card, running its own operating system as if it were on real hardware.

children.title: Host vs guest
children.desc: The host is the physical machine (or the hypervisor on it). The guest is the operating system running inside the VM, which usually does not know it is virtual.

children.title: Virtual hardware
children.desc: vCPUs, vRAM, virtual disks, virtual network adapters, and virtual BIOS/UEFI. Each can be resized without touching physical hardware.

children.title: A VM is files
children.desc: On ESXi a VM is a folder: .vmx holds the configuration, .vmdk the disk, .nvram the firmware settings, vmware.log the VM's log. Copying the files copies the machine.

children.title: Snapshot
children.desc: A point-in-time state of the disk (and optionally memory). Useful before changes, but not a backup: it lives on the same storage and slows the VM if kept for long.

children.title: Template & clone
children.desc: A template is a master VM used to create identical new ones. OVF/OVA is the portable format for moving VMs between platforms.

children.title: Guest tools
children.desc: Drivers installed inside the guest (VMware Tools, Hyper-V integration services) for better performance, clean shutdown, and reporting the guest's IP and hostname to the hypervisor.

modules.title: Type 1 Hypervisor
modules.desc: Installed directly on the physical server with no general-purpose operating system underneath. The hypervisor is the operating system of the host.

children.title: How it works
children.desc: Hardware → hypervisor → VMs. The hypervisor talks to the hardware itself and schedules CPU and memory among the VMs.

children.title: Examples
children.desc: VMware ESXi, Microsoft Hyper-V, Xen, and KVM-based platforms such as Proxmox VE and Nutanix AHV.

children.title: Strengths
children.desc: Best performance, small attack surface, high stability. Built for data centers and production workloads.

children.title: Trade-offs
children.desc: Needs a dedicated server and is managed remotely through a web or management console, not by sitting at the machine.

children.title: Hyper-V nuance
children.desc: Even when enabled on Windows, Hyper-V is Type 1: it loads beneath Windows, which then itself runs as a privileged partition.

modules.title: Type 2 Hypervisor
modules.desc: Installed as an application on top of a normal operating system such as Windows, macOS, or Linux.

children.title: How it works
children.desc: Hardware → host OS → hypervisor application → VMs. Every hardware request goes through the host operating system.

children.title: Examples
children.desc: Oracle VirtualBox, VMware Workstation, VMware Fusion, Parallels Desktop.

children.title: Strengths
children.desc: Easy to install on a laptop, ideal for personal labs, testing, training, and running another OS alongside your own.

children.title: Trade-offs
children.desc: Extra layer means lower performance, and the VMs depend on the host OS — if it crashes or is compromised, they are affected too.

modules.title: Container Virtualization
modules.desc: Virtualizes the operating system rather than the hardware. Containers share the host's kernel and are isolated from each other only by kernel features. See the Containers & Kubernetes map for depth.

children.title: How it works
children.desc: Hardware → host OS and kernel → container runtime → containers. Each container holds only the application and its libraries, not a whole operating system.

children.title: Isolation mechanism
children.desc: Linux namespaces give each container its own view of processes, network, and filesystem; cgroups limit its CPU and memory.

children.title: Examples
children.desc: Docker, containerd, Podman, and Kubernetes to orchestrate them at scale.

children.title: Strengths
children.desc: Megabytes instead of gigabytes, starts in seconds, packs far more workloads per host, and runs the same everywhere.

children.title: Trade-offs
children.desc: Weaker isolation than a VM: a kernel vulnerability can affect every container on the host. Containers must use the host's kernel type — Linux containers need a Linux kernel.

modules.title: Side by Side
modules.desc: The core differences in one place — what sits under the workload, and what that means for performance and isolation.

children.title: What is virtualized
children.desc: Type 1 and Type 2 virtualize hardware, so each VM runs a full OS. Containers virtualize the OS, so they share one kernel.

children.title: What runs underneath
children.desc: Type 1: nothing but the hypervisor. Type 2: a full host OS. Container: the host OS kernel plus a runtime.

children.title: Performance & size
children.desc: Containers are lightest, Type 1 is close to physical speed, Type 2 carries the most overhead.

children.title: Isolation strength
children.desc: Type 1 strongest, Type 2 depends on the host OS, containers weakest because of the shared kernel.

children.title: Typical use
children.desc: Type 1: production data centers. Type 2: personal labs and desktops. Containers: microservices and cloud-native apps, often running inside VMs on a Type 1 hypervisor.

modules.title: VMware ESXi
modules.desc: VMware's Type 1 hypervisor and the most widespread in enterprise data centers. A small, purpose-built OS whose core is the VMkernel; it does nothing except run VMs.

children.title: VMkernel
children.desc: The ESXi core that schedules CPU, manages memory, and handles storage and network I/O for every VM on the host.

children.title: Host Client
children.desc: The web interface of a single host, reached in a browser at https://<host-ip>/ui. Used to create VMs, configure networking and storage, and open VM consoles.

children.title: DCUI
children.desc: The text console on the physical server's screen (F2), used for initial setup: management IP, root password, enabling troubleshooting services.

children.title: vCenter Server
children.desc: Central management for many ESXi hosts. Adds clusters, vMotion (live migration), HA (automatic restart on host failure), DRS (load balancing), and templates.

children.title: vSphere
children.desc: The product family name: ESXi hypervisors plus vCenter together.

children.title: Ownership
children.desc: Broadcom acquired VMware in 2023 and moved licensing to subscriptions, which pushed some organizations to evaluate alternatives such as Proxmox, Nutanix, or Hyper-V.

modules.title: ESXi Networking
modules.desc: VMs connect to virtual switches inside the host, which connect to the physical network through the host's real network cards.

children.title: Uplinks
children.desc: The host's physical NICs (vmnic0, vmnic1…). They connect the virtual switch to the physical network; two or more give redundancy.

children.title: Standard vSwitch
children.desc: A software switch on one host. vSwitch0 is created at install time.

children.title: Port group
children.desc: A named set of ports on a vSwitch with shared settings, usually a VLAN ID. A VM's network adapter is attached to a port group, which decides which network segment it is on.

children.title: VMkernel port
children.desc: A network interface for the host itself rather than for VMs: management traffic, vMotion, storage. The management IP lives here.

children.title: Distributed switch
children.desc: With vCenter, one switch configuration spans many hosts, so a VM keeps the same network settings when it moves.

modules.title: ESXi Storage
modules.desc: Where VM files live. ESXi presents every kind of storage — local disks, SAN, NAS — as a datastore.

children.title: Datastore
children.desc: A storage container that holds VM folders, ISO images, and templates.

children.title: VMFS
children.desc: VMware's cluster file system for block storage (local disks, Fibre Channel, iSCSI). Several hosts can use the same datastore at once.

children.title: NFS / vSAN
children.desc: NFS mounts network file shares as datastores. vSAN pools the local disks of several hosts into one shared datastore.

children.title: Thin vs thick
children.desc: A thin disk uses space only as data is written; a thick disk reserves its full size up front. Thin saves space but risks running out if overcommitted.

modules.title: Creating a VM
modules.desc: The basic flow in the ESXi Host Client. vCenter offers the same wizard with extra placement options.

children.title: 1. Start the wizard
children.desc: Virtual Machines → Create / Register VM → Create a new virtual machine.

children.title: 2. Name & guest OS
children.desc: Give the VM a name, choose the compatibility version, and select the guest OS family and version so ESXi picks suitable virtual hardware.

children.title: 3. Storage
children.desc: Choose the datastore that will hold the VM's folder and disks.

children.title: 4. Customize hardware
children.desc: Set vCPUs, memory, disk size and thin/thick provisioning, network adapter type (VMXNET3) and port group, and attach an installation ISO from a datastore to the CD/DVD drive.

children.title: 5. Install the OS
children.desc: Power on, open the web console, and install the guest operating system from the ISO as on a physical machine.

children.title: 6. Finish setup
children.desc: Install VMware Tools, set the IP address, patch, and take a snapshot or convert to a template if more copies will be needed.

modules.title: ESXi in the SOC
modules.desc: One ESXi host can run dozens of critical servers, so it is one of the most valuable targets in a network and needs its own monitoring.

children.title: High-value target
children.desc: Compromising the hypervisor reaches every VM on it at once. Several ransomware groups ship ESXi-specific versions that encrypt the VM disk files directly.

children.title: Visibility gap
children.desc: Standard endpoint agents run inside the guest VMs, not on the ESXi host itself. Host activity is visible mainly through ESXi and vCenter logs.

children.title: Logs to collect
children.desc: Forward ESXi syslog to the SIEM: hostd.log (management actions), vmkernel.log, auth.log and shell.log (logins and shell commands), plus vCenter events.

children.title: What to watch
children.desc: Logins to the Host Client or SSH from unusual sources, SSH or the ESXi shell being enabled, new local accounts, mass VM power-offs, and snapshot or datastore deletions.

children.title: Hardening
children.desc: Management interfaces only on an isolated management network, SSH off by default, lockdown mode, prompt patching, and vCenter access tied to named accounts with MFA.

children.title: Forensics
children.desc: A snapshot with memory captures a running VM's RAM and disk without shutting it down — useful evidence during an investigation.
